sections.title: 1. Purpose and place in the outline

blocks.text: Grade 3 is the Colonial year of the four-year cycle (§4): exploration, settlement, the founding, the early republic and westward expansion, from about 1600 to 1850. Geography is built in, with map work every week and the fifty states and their capitals as the year's geography goal (§3C). The timeline notebook, begun in Grade 1, gets new entries every week (§3C).

At the grammar stage, history is the story and the facts: who, what, when and where. The "why" questions belong mostly to the logic stage (§1). This course fills the storehouse: names, dates, places and events, told as a story and fixed on a map and a timeline.

History and Literature share the period (§4) but do different jobs. Literature reads the living books, biographies and poems: Pocahontas, Franklin, Washington, Lincoln. History tells the whole story around them, in order, with the map and the dates. The two courses follow the same six themes, term by term.

blocks.text: Order within the week: A first; B, C and D in any order after it.
36 weeks in 6 six-week terms.
4 tasks a week, so 24 per term, all in the weekly queue.
Expected time: about 2–2½ hours a week.

Spine: This Country of Ours by H. E. Marshall (1917, public domain, free online). It tells American history as a story, in short chapters, from the explorers to the modern era. Each term manual names the chapters for each week.
Alternative: The Story of the Thirteen Colonies and the Great Republic by H. A. Guerber (1898, public domain), for families who prefer it.
Read as written. Both books are read as their authors wrote them, without added commentary. Questions of interpretation belong to the logic and rhetoric stages (§1), not the grammar stage.

Primary sources (task D) are short and read together: lines from the Mayflower Compact, a colonial advertisement, a soldier's letter, a few sentences of the Declaration. Literature already covers the Preamble and the Declaration's opening for recitation; History looks at them as historical documents.
The themes match Literature term for term, so each family reads the story and the history of the same period at the same time.

sections.title: 5. Geography: the fifty states and capitals

blocks.text: The outline names states and capitals as Grade 3 geography (§3C). They're learned by region, timed to the history where possible, about eight or nine states a term.

blocks.text: Daily drill happens in Memory Work (11), which chants the states and capitals in the daily core. This course places them on the map once a week.
Each term's map check covers that term's states and all earlier ones.

Also on the map this year: the oceans and continents (review from Grade 1), the thirteen colonies, major rivers (Mississippi, Missouri, Ohio, Hudson, Columbia), the Appalachian and Rocky Mountains, and the routes of the year (the Mayflower, Revere's ride, Lewis and Clark, the Oregon Trail).
Every week adds two or three dated events, each with a short label and a small drawing.
The notebook runs from Grade 1 (§3C). Grade 3's pages begin at 1492, as a doorway, and run to 1850.
Presidents: the first twelve presidents (Washington to Taylor) are added as they come, and their names go into the Memory Work queue in order.
Once a term, the child reads their timeline pages aloud from the start of the year. That's the timeline review.
Narration (task A): weekly and oral, not graded. The parent notes one strong detail and one gap, as in Literature.

Term map check (week 6 of each term): a blank outline map. The child labels the term's states and capitals and all earlier ones, plus the term's other places. 90% correct is the term standard. Missed states go back into the Memory Work rotation.

Term timeline check (week 6): the parent reads out six events from the term in jumbled order; the child puts them in order and says roughly when each happened. Not scored; any confusion is noted for review.

Year-end standard (week 36): locate all fifty states on a blank map and name at least 45 of their capitals, and tell the story of the period in order, from Jamestown to the Gold Rush, in a few minutes of oral narration.
Written narration happens in task D in some weeks. It isn't marked for spelling or grammar (those belong to courses 03 and 02).
Portfolio: the timeline notebook, the term maps and written narrations carry forward (§8).

head: Course
Link
rows: Same six themes; Literature reads the biographies and poems, History tells the surrounding story. Term themes match by design
Timeline subtraction (1620 − 1607); word problems set in the period
Colonial trades in Term 2 (candle-making, soap, dyeing) are early chemistry. Science can borrow them as demonstrations
Church history: the Pilgrims' and Puritans' faith, William Penn and the Quakers, the Great Awakening
States and capitals chant; the timeline dates; the presidents in order
Colonial folk art and portraiture (§4): portraits of Washington and Franklin in this course's reading
Colonial work like candle-dipping, butter-churning and simple tools makes good task D projects, and fits the Workshop and Hearth tracks (§6)
History supplies examples of each virtue in the period. Order: Faith and Hope, Temperance, Fortitude, Justice, Prudence, Charity

blocks.text: The period includes slavery, the removal of Native nations and war. At this grade they're told as the sources tell them: plainly, briefly and without added commentary, at a level a young child can carry. Discussion and interpretation come later, in the logic and rhetoric stages (§1).
Content work carries over freely (§7). A missed week moves the reading forward and doesn't need to be made up.
States and capitals are cumulative, but the daily drill lives in Memory Work, so a missed week of map work costs little.
The term's review week absorbs one missed week.

sections.title: 11. What each term manual will contain

blocks.text: For each week: the spine chapters, a narration prompt, the map task (places and states), the timeline entries, and the task D activity. For each term: the term map check with an answer list, and the timeline check events.

terms.title: Theme: Exploration and First Settlements

head: Spine
This Country of Ours, H. E. Marshall: the opening chapters on the explorers, the Virginia chapters, and the New England chapters
rows: Why Europeans crossed the ocean · Roanoke and the Native peoples of the coast · Jamestown · the Pilgrims and the Mayflower · Plymouth, the Puritans and Rhode Island · review
Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Connecticut, Virginia, Maryland, Massachusetts, Rhode Island (8)
Literature reads Pocahontas, Stories of the Pilgrims and The Courage of Sarah Noble this term

glance.text: Finding the chapters. Chapter numbers differ between editions of This Country of Ours, and the book is free online in several versions. Each week names the chapters by subject; use the table of contents to find them. The book is read as Marshall wrote it.
Order each week. A first; then B, C and D in any order.

Before week 1. Have a large outline map of the United States, a world map or globe, colored pencils, and the timeline notebook from Grade 2. Start this year's timeline pages with a title page: The Colonial Years, 1492–1850.

blocks.text: The opening chapters on the explorers: Columbus and the voyages that followed. Narrate: "What was Columbus looking for, and what did he find instead?"

On the world map: trace Columbus's route from Spain across the Atlantic to the islands of the Caribbean. Label Europe, North America, South America and the Atlantic Ocean. On the U.S. map: Maine (Augusta), New Hampshire (Concord).
Title page for the year. 1492: Columbus crosses the Atlantic.

Make a simple compass: rub a sewing needle on a magnet 30 times in one direction, push it through a small piece of cork, and float it in a bowl of water. It turns to point north, as explorers' compasses did.

weeks.title: Roanoke and the peoples of the coast

blocks.text: The chapters on Sir Walter Raleigh and the Roanoke colonies, including the "Lost Colony" of 1587. Narrate: "What happened to the colony at Roanoke? What word was found carved on a post?"
Label Roanoke Island off the coast of North Carolina, and the Atlantic coast from Maine to Virginia. States: Vermont (Montpelier), Connecticut (Hartford).
1587: The Roanoke colony is founded, and later vanishes.
Build a small model of a coastal village house from sticks and paper or bark, the way the peoples of the coast built their homes, using the descriptions and pictures in the reading.
The Virginia chapters: the founding of Jamestown, Captain John Smith, Powhatan and Pocahontas, the "starving time", and tobacco. Narrate: "How did Captain John Smith keep the colony alive?"
Label Chesapeake Bay, the James River and Jamestown. States: Virginia (Richmond), Maryland (Annapolis).
1607: Jamestown, the first lasting English settlement. 1619: Virginia's first elected assembly meets; the first Africans arrive in Virginia.

Read John Smith's rule for the colony: "He that will not work shall not eat." Talk about what it meant for a colony where many men didn't want to farm. The child copies it in their best handwriting for the timeline page.

The New England chapters: the Pilgrims in England and Holland, the voyage of the Mayflower, and the Mayflower Compact. Narrate: "Why did the Pilgrims leave England? What did the men agree to before they left the ship?"
Trace the Mayflower's route from Plymouth, England, to Cape Cod. Label Cape Cod and Plymouth. State: Massachusetts (Boston).
1620: The Mayflower lands; the Mayflower Compact is signed.

Read the opening of the Mayflower Compact: "In the name of God, Amen. We whose names are underwritten…" and the part where they agree to "combine ourselves together into a civil body politic". Explain "civil body politic" simply: a group of people who agree to make and keep their own laws. The child narrates what the Compact promised.

weeks.title: Plymouth, the Puritans and Rhode Island

blocks.text: The chapters on the first winter at Plymouth, Samoset and Squanto, the treaty with Massasoit and the harvest feast; then the Puritans at Massachusetts Bay under John Winthrop, and Roger Williams founding Rhode Island. Narrate: "How did Squanto help the Pilgrims?"
Label Massachusetts Bay, Boston and Providence. State: Rhode Island (Providence).
1621: The Pilgrims' harvest feast. 1630: The Puritans found Boston. 1636: Roger Williams founds Providence.
3–6 sentences in cursive: "The Pilgrims' first year at Plymouth." Not marked for spelling or grammar.

Correct order: Columbus (1492) · Roanoke (1587) · Jamestown (1607) · Plymouth (1620) · Boston (1630) · Providence (1636).

blocks.text: The child reads the term's timeline pages aloud from 1492 to 1636, telling the story at each date.

The parent reads the six events below in jumbled order; the child puts them in order and gives the dates they remember.
The child's choice from the term: finish a map, add drawings to the timeline, or make a model of the Mayflower or a Jamestown fort.

Literature and History overlap on purpose. The child meets Pocahontas and the Pilgrims in both courses this term: as a story in Literature, and as history, with dates and a map, here. That doubling helps the facts stick.
States are drilled daily in Memory Work. This course places them on the map once a week. If a state isn't sticking, ask Memory Work to give it an extra day.
Keep narration short. Two or three minutes is plenty. The goal is that the child can tell what happened in order, not that they remember every detail.

terms.title: Theme: Colonial Life and Work

head: Spine
This Country of Ours, H. E. Marshall: the chapters on New Netherland and New York, the New England colonies, William Penn and Pennsylvania, the Carolinas and Georgia, and the French and Indian War
rows: The thirteen colonies in three regions · New England towns and trades · the Middle colonies and William Penn · the Southern colonies · Georgia and the French and Indian War · review
New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia (7 new; 15 in all)
Literature reads Benjamin Franklin, Ox-Cart Man and Ben and Me this term

glance.text: Finding the chapters. Chapter numbers differ between editions; use the table of contents. The book is read as Marshall wrote it.
Order each week. A first; then B, C and D in any order.

blocks.text: The chapters on New Netherland: the Dutch on the Hudson River, the purchase of Manhattan, and the English taking New Amsterdam and naming it New York. Narrate: "How did New Amsterdam become New York?"

Color the thirteen colonies in three regions: New England (New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut), Middle (New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware), Southern (Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia). Label the Hudson River and Manhattan. State: New York (Albany).
1626: The Dutch buy Manhattan. 1664: New Amsterdam becomes New York.
Make a large poster map of the thirteen colonies, one color per region, to hang up for the rest of the year.
The chapters on life in the New England colonies: the town and its meetinghouse, farms, fishing, shipbuilding, the town school. Narrate: "What would a child in a New England town do in a day?"
Label Boston, Salem and the fishing grounds off Cape Cod. State: New Jersey (Trenton).
1647: Massachusetts requires towns to keep schools.

Candle-dipping (with an adult at every step): dip a wick in melted wax, let it cool, and dip again, twenty times or more. This is how colonial families made light. It pairs with Science's chemistry year, and with Ox-Cart Man in Literature.

weeks.title: The Middle colonies and William Penn

blocks.text: The chapters on William Penn: the Quakers, the founding of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, and Penn's treaty with the Lenape. Narrate: "Why did William Penn found Pennsylvania? What does 'Philadelphia' mean?"
Label the Delaware River and Philadelphia. States: Pennsylvania (Harrisburg), Delaware (Dover).
1681: William Penn receives Pennsylvania. 1682: Penn makes a treaty with the Lenape.
3–6 sentences in cursive: "William Penn and Pennsylvania." Note that Ben Franklin, in Literature this term, made Philadelphia his home.

The chapters on Maryland and the Carolinas: large farms called plantations, and the crops grown there (tobacco, rice and indigo), worked by enslaved Africans and by servants; the port of Charles Town. Narrate: "What crops were grown in the Southern colonies, and how were they sent to England?"
Label Charles Town (now Charleston) and the coast of the Carolinas. States: North Carolina (Raleigh), South Carolina (Columbia).
1670: Charles Town is founded in Carolina.
Colonial dyeing: dye a piece of white cotton cloth with onion skins boiled in water (yellow-brown), with an adult at the stove. Indigo gave the colonists blue the same way. Another link to Science.

weeks.title: Georgia and the French and Indian War

blocks.text: The chapters on James Oglethorpe founding Georgia, and on the French and Indian War: France and Britain fighting over the Ohio country, young George Washington's first command, and the British victory. Narrate: "What were France and Britain fighting over? Who won?"
Label Savannah, the Ohio River, Quebec and French Canada. State: Georgia (Atlanta).
1732: Georgia, the thirteenth colony, is founded. 1754: The French and Indian War begins. 1763: The war ends; France gives up Canada.

Show Ben Franklin's 1754 cartoon Join, or Die: a snake cut into pieces, each labeled with a colony. Talk about what Franklin meant. (It matches the fable The Bundle of Sticks, coming in Literature next term.)

weeks.title: Review, map check and timeline check

intro.text: Map check answers (week 12)
Also on the map: New England, Middle and Southern regions · Philadelphia · Charleston · Hudson River · Ohio River.
Standard: 90% correct (27 of the 30 state and capital labels). Missed states go back into the Memory Work rotation.
Timeline check events
Read in this jumbled order: Penn receives Pennsylvania · The Dutch buy Manhattan · The French and Indian War ends · Georgia is founded · Charles Town is founded · New Amsterdam becomes New York.
Correct order: Manhattan (1626) · New York (1664) · Charles Town (1670) · Pennsylvania (1681) · Georgia (1732) · end of the war (1763).

blocks.text: The child reads the term's timeline pages aloud, telling the story at each date. Then they name the three regions of the colonies and one thing each region was known for.
On a blank outline map: label all 15 states and capitals learned so far, plus the three colonial regions, Philadelphia, Charleston and the Hudson and Ohio Rivers. Answer list below.
Jumbled events below; the child puts them in order.
The child's choice: finish the colonies poster, make a New England primer page, or dip more candles.
The three regions are the term's big idea. If the child can say where each colony is and what each region did (fishing and trade, grain and cities, plantations and crops), the term has done its work.
Projects need an adult. Candle-dipping and dyeing use heat. Keep the child at a safe distance from the stove and let them do the dipping and stirring.
States are cumulative. The week 12 map check includes Term 1's eight states. If several are shaky, spend a few Memory Work days on them before Term 3.

terms.title: Theme: Road to Revolution

head: Spine
This Country of Ours, H. E. Marshall: the chapters on the quarrel with Britain and the War of Independence
rows: The Stamp Act · the Boston Massacre and the Tea Party · Lexington and Concord · the Declaration and the war · Yorktown and peace · review
Kentucky, Tennessee, West Virginia, Alabama, Mississippi, Florida, Louisiana, Arkansas (8 new; 23 in all)
Literature reads George Washington, And Then What Happened, Paul Revere? and Sam the Minuteman this term

glance.text: About this term's states. The states this term lie south and west of the thirteen colonies, in lands that would be settled after the war. They're learned now to keep pace with the year's fifty; Term 5 tells how settlers moved into them.
Finding the chapters. Chapter numbers differ between editions; use the table of contents. The book is read as Marshall wrote it.
Order each week. A first; then B, C and D in any order.

blocks.text: The chapters on Britain's new taxes after the French and Indian War, the Stamp Act, the colonists' protests, and its repeal. Narrate: "Why did Britain want to tax the colonies? Why were the colonists angry?"
Draw a line across the Atlantic from London to Boston. States: Kentucky (Frankfort), Tennessee (Nashville).
1765: The Stamp Act. 1766: The Stamp Act is repealed.

The colonists' slogan: "No taxation without representation." Explain each word, and what the colonists meant: they had no vote in Parliament, which taxed them. The child designs their own tax stamp, like the ones the law required on newspapers and papers.

weeks.title: The Boston Massacre and the Tea Party

blocks.text: The chapters on soldiers in Boston, the Boston Massacre, the tax on tea, and the Boston Tea Party. Narrate: "Tell what happened on the night of the Tea Party, in order."
Draw Boston and its harbor; mark Griffin's Wharf, where the tea ships were. State: West Virginia (Charleston). Not the same as Charleston, South Carolina, from Term 2.
1770: The Boston Massacre. 1773: The Boston Tea Party.
3–6 sentences in cursive: "The Boston Tea Party."

The chapters on the closing of Boston's port, the First Continental Congress, Paul Revere's ride, the fighting at Lexington and Concord, and Bunker Hill. Narrate: "What did Paul Revere and William Dawes ride to warn people about?"
Trace the routes of Revere and Dawes from Boston to Lexington, and the British march to Concord. States: Alabama (Montgomery), Mississippi (Jackson).
1774: The First Continental Congress. 1775: Lexington and Concord; the war begins.

Read the first stanza of Ralph Waldo Emerson's "Concord Hymn" (1837), which calls the first shot at Concord "the shot heard round the world." The child memorizes that one line. It pairs with Literature's "Paul Revere's Ride".

The chapters on Washington taking command, the Declaration of Independence, the crossing of the Delaware and the victory at Trenton, the battle of Saratoga and France joining the war, and the winter at Valley Forge. Narrate: "Why was Saratoga so important?"
Label Philadelphia, Trenton, the Delaware River, Saratoga and Valley Forge. State: Florida (Tallahassee).
1776: The Declaration of Independence (July 4); Washington crosses the Delaware (December 25). 1777: Saratoga. 1778: France joins the war; the army leaves Valley Forge.

Read the Declaration's closing words: "we mutually pledge to each other our Lives, our Fortunes and our sacred Honor." Talk about what the signers were risking. (Literature recites a different line of the Declaration in Term 4.)
The chapters on the war in the South, the siege of Yorktown with the French army and fleet, the British surrender, and the Treaty of Paris. Narrate: "How did the war end? How did the French help?"
Label Yorktown, Virginia. Draw the borders of the new United States in 1783: the Atlantic to the Mississippi River, Canada to Florida. States: Louisiana (Baton Rouge), Arkansas (Little Rock).
1781: The British surrender at Yorktown. 1783: The Treaty of Paris; Britain recognizes the United States.
Make a map of the United States in 1783, colored inside its new borders, and compare it with the thirteen colonies poster from Term 2. How much bigger is the new country?

terms.title: Theme: Founding the Republic

head: Spine
This Country of Ours, H. E. Marshall: the chapters after the war on the new government, the Constitution, and the presidencies of Washington, Adams and Jefferson
rows: The Articles of Confederation and the Northwest Ordinance · the Constitutional Convention · the three branches and the Bill of Rights · Washington, Adams and the new capital · Jefferson and the Louisiana Purchase · review
Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa, Missouri (8 new; 31 in all)
1. George Washington (1789) · 2. John Adams (1797) · 3. Thomas Jefferson (1801)
Literature reads Will You Sign Here, John Hancock?, Shh! We're Writing the Constitution and Toliver's Secret this term

glance.text: About this term's states. These are the states of the old Northwest Territory and the Mississippi valley. The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 (week 19) set out how that land would become states, which makes this the right term to learn them.
Finding the chapters. Chapter numbers differ between editions; use the table of contents. The book is read as Marshall wrote it.
Order each week. A first; then B, C and D in any order.

weeks.title: The Articles of Confederation and the Northwest Ordinance

blocks.text: The chapters on the years after the war: the Articles of Confederation, a weak government that couldn't collect taxes or settle quarrels between the states; Shays' Rebellion in Massachusetts; and the Northwest Ordinance, the plan for the land north of the Ohio River. Narrate: "Why was the government under the Articles too weak?"
Shade the Northwest Territory: the land between the Ohio River, the Mississippi and the Great Lakes. Label the five Great Lakes. States: Ohio (Columbus), Indiana (Indianapolis).
1781: The Articles of Confederation take effect. 1786: Shays' Rebellion. 1787: The Northwest Ordinance.

A quick demonstration of the Articles' problem: give each member of the family a vote on something, and require all of them to agree before anything can be done. Then talk about why thirteen states found it hard to agree on anything.

The chapters on the Convention in Philadelphia: Washington presiding, James Madison's plan, Franklin, the quarrel between large and small states, the Great Compromise, and the signing on September 17, 1787. Narrate: "What was the Great Compromise?"
Label Philadelphia and mark Independence Hall. States: Illinois (Springfield), Michigan (Lansing).
1787: The Constitution is signed (September 17).

At the end of the Convention, Franklin pointed to the sun carved on the back of Washington's chair and said that he now knew it was a rising sun, not a setting one. Tell the story, then ask: what did Franklin mean about the new country?

weeks.title: The three branches and the Bill of Rights

blocks.text: The chapters on how the new government works, or a short parent explanation if the spine gives only a little. Three branches: Congress makes the laws; the President carries out the laws; the courts judge the laws. Each branch can check the others. Then the Bill of Rights, the first ten amendments, adding freedoms such as freedom of religion, of speech and of the press. Narrate: "What does each branch do?"
Label New York City, the first capital. States: Wisconsin (Madison), Minnesota (Saint Paul).
1791: The Bill of Rights is added to the Constitution.
Draw a tree with three branches. Label them Congress, President and Courts, with a picture on each of what it does. Write "The Constitution" on the trunk.

weeks.title: Washington, Adams and the new capital

blocks.text: The chapters on George Washington as the first president, taking the oath in New York, his two terms and his return to Mount Vernon; John Adams, the second president; and the new capital city on the Potomac, named for Washington. Narrate: "Why did Washington go home after two terms?"
Label the Potomac River, Washington, D.C., and Mount Vernon. State: Iowa (Des Moines).
1789: George Washington becomes the first president. 1797: John Adams becomes president. 1800: The government moves to Washington, D.C. Add Washington and Adams to the presidents page.
3–6 sentences in cursive: "George Washington, the first president."
The chapters on Thomas Jefferson as the third president, and the Louisiana Purchase from France in 1803, which doubled the size of the country. Narrate: "What did Jefferson buy, and from whom?"
Shade the Louisiana Purchase, from the Mississippi to the Rocky Mountains. Label New Orleans, St. Louis and the Missouri River. State: Missouri (Jefferson City).
1801: Thomas Jefferson becomes president. 1803: The Louisiana Purchase. Add Jefferson to the presidents page.
On the 1783 map from Term 3, color in the Louisiana Purchase in a new color. Ask: how much bigger is the country now? It sets up next term, when Jefferson sends Lewis and Clark to explore it.

terms.title: Theme: Westward Expansion

head: Spine
This Country of Ours, H. E. Marshall: the chapters on the pioneers, Lewis and Clark, the War of 1812, and the presidents through Andrew Jackson
rows: Daniel Boone and the Wilderness Road · Lewis and Clark · the War of 1812 · steamboats and the Erie Canal · the Trail of Tears · review
Nebraska, Kansas, North Dakota, South Dakota, Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, Washington, Oregon (9 new; 40 in all)
4. James Madison (1809) · 5. James Monroe (1817) · 6. John Quincy Adams (1825) · 7. Andrew Jackson (1829)
Literature reads American Tall Tales, Johnny Appleseed and How We Crossed the West this term

glance.text: Finding the chapters. Chapter numbers differ between editions; use the table of contents. The book is read as Marshall wrote it.
Order each week. A first; then B, C and D in any order.

weeks.title: Daniel Boone and the Wilderness Road

blocks.text: The chapters on Daniel Boone: the Cumberland Gap, blazing the Wilderness Road, and the settlement at Boonesborough in Kentucky. Narrate: "How did settlers get across the mountains into Kentucky?"
Label the Appalachian Mountains, the Cumberland Gap and the Wilderness Road into Kentucky. States: Nebraska (Lincoln), Kansas (Topeka).
1775: Daniel Boone blazes the Wilderness Road. 1792: Kentucky becomes a state.
Pack a pioneer's load: list what a family could carry over the mountains on foot and by pack horse, then choose the ten most important things.

The chapters on the Corps of Discovery: setting out from St. Louis, the winter with the Mandan, Sacagawea, crossing the Rockies, reaching the Pacific and the journey home. Narrate: "What were Lewis and Clark sent to find?"
Trace the route: St. Louis, up the Missouri River, across the Rocky Mountains, down the Columbia River to the Pacific. States: North Dakota (Bismarck), South Dakota (Pierre).
1804: Lewis and Clark set out. 1805: They reach the Pacific. 1806: They return to St. Louis.
Read Clark's journal line "Ocian in view! O! the joy." (November 1805), with his own spelling. The child copied it in Penmanship this term too. Talk about how long they had traveled to see it.

The chapters on the War of 1812 under President Madison: British ships stopping American sailors, the burning of Washington, the defense of Fort McHenry and Francis Scott Key's song, and Andrew Jackson at New Orleans. Narrate: "What did Francis Scott Key see that made him write his song?"
Label Baltimore and Fort McHenry, Washington, D.C., and New Orleans. States: Montana (Helena), Idaho (Boise).
1812: The War of 1812 begins. 1814: Washington is burned; "The Star-Spangled Banner" is written. 1815: The Battle of New Orleans. Add James Madison (1809) to the presidents page.
Read the first verse of "The Star-Spangled Banner" and talk through what it describes: the night, the rockets, and the flag still flying at dawn. The child memorizes the first four lines.

The chapters on new ways of traveling: Robert Fulton's steamboat on the Hudson, the Erie Canal from Albany to Buffalo, roads west, and the first railroads. Narrate: "Why was the Erie Canal so important?"
Trace the Erie Canal from Albany to Buffalo and Lake Erie. Label the Hudson River. State: Wyoming (Cheyenne).
1807: Fulton's steamboat. 1825: The Erie Canal opens. Add James Monroe (1817) and John Quincy Adams (1825) to the presidents page.
Make a simple canal in a rain gutter or a long tray of water, and float a small boat along it pulled by a string, the way mules pulled canal boats along the towpath.

The chapters on President Andrew Jackson and the Indian Removal Act, under which the Cherokee and other nations were moved from the Southeast to Indian Territory, west of the Mississippi. The Cherokee's journey in 1838 became known as the Trail of Tears; many died along the way. Narrate: "Where were the Cherokee moved from, and where to?"
Trace the route from Georgia and Tennessee west to Indian Territory (today's Oklahoma). States: Washington (Olympia), Oregon (Salem).
1830: The Indian Removal Act. 1838: The Trail of Tears. Add Andrew Jackson (1829) to the presidents page.
3–6 sentences in cursive: "How people traveled west, from the Wilderness Road to the Erie Canal."

terms.title: Theme: To 1850 — Bridge to the Modern Year

head: Spine
This Country of Ours, H. E. Marshall: the chapters on the Oregon Trail, Texas, the Mexican War, California and the years before 1850
rows: The Oregon and Mormon Trails · Texas and the Alamo · the Mexican War and the Gold Rush · the Underground Railroad · the country in 1850 · year review
Colorado, Utah, Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Arizona, Nevada, California, Alaska, Hawaii (10 new; all 50)
8. Martin Van Buren (1837) · 9. William Henry Harrison (1841) · 10. John Tyler (1841) · 11. James K. Polk (1845) · 12. Zachary Taylor (1849)
Literature reads the d'Aulaires' Abraham Lincoln this term, which carries on past 1850 into the Civil War

glance.text: Where History stops. History ends at 1850, the close of the Colonial period on the four-year cycle (§4). Literature's Lincoln book goes further, through the Civil War. That's fine: Grade 4's Modern year begins with the Civil War, and the child will meet it again there in full.
Finding the chapters. Chapter numbers differ between editions; use the table of contents. The book is read as Marshall wrote it.
Order each week. A first; then B, C and D in any order.

blocks.text: The chapters on the wagon trains to Oregon: setting out from Independence, Missouri, the long trail across the plains and mountains, and the settlers' arrival in the Oregon country. Then the Mormon pioneers' journey to the Great Salt Lake valley. Narrate: "What was a day like on the Oregon Trail?"
Trace the Oregon Trail from Independence, Missouri, to Oregon City, and the Mormon Trail to the Great Salt Lake. States: Colorado (Denver), Utah (Salt Lake City).
1843: The great migration on the Oregon Trail. 1847: Mormon pioneers reach the Great Salt Lake. Add Martin Van Buren (1837) to the presidents page.
Plan a wagon: a covered wagon could carry about 2,000 pounds. List what a family would pack (food, tools, clothing) and estimate the weight of each. Link to Arithmetic: adding to 2,000.

The chapters on Americans settling in Texas, then part of Mexico; the Texas Revolution; the defense of the Alamo, with Davy Crockett and Jim Bowie; Sam Houston's victory at San Jacinto; the Republic of Texas; and Texas becoming a state. Narrate: "What happened at the Alamo?"
Label San Antonio (the Alamo), the Rio Grande and the Republic of Texas. States: Texas (Austin), Oklahoma (Oklahoma City).
1836: The Alamo; Texas wins independence. 1845: Texas becomes a state. Add William Henry Harrison and John Tyler (both 1841) and James K. Polk (1845) to the presidents page.
The cry at San Jacinto: "Remember the Alamo!" Davy Crockett appeared in Literature's tall tales in Term 5; talk about the difference between the legend and the real man.

weeks.title: The Mexican War and the Gold Rush

blocks.text: The chapters on the war with Mexico under President Polk, the lands of the Southwest and California added to the country, and the discovery of gold at Sutter's Mill that began the California Gold Rush. Narrate: "Why did so many people rush to California in 1849?"

Shade the land added after the Mexican War, from Texas to California. Label Sutter's Mill and San Francisco. States: New Mexico (Santa Fe), Arizona (Phoenix), Nevada (Carson City), California (Sacramento).
1846: The war with Mexico begins. 1848: Gold is found at Sutter's Mill; the war ends. 1849: The Gold Rush. Add Zachary Taylor (1849) to the presidents page.
Pan for "gold": mix a few small painted pebbles into sand and gravel in a pan of water, and swirl the water to wash the lighter sand away, the way the forty-niners did.

The chapters, or a short parent reading, on the Underground Railroad: the secret routes by which enslaved people escaped from the South to the free states and Canada, guided by the North Star and helped by people along the way. Frederick Douglass escaped and became a famous speaker; Harriet Tubman escaped in 1849 and went back many times to lead others to freedom. Narrate: "How did Harriet Tubman find her way north?"

Mark the free states and the slave states in 1850 in two colors; draw arrows north toward Canada. Find the North Star in a picture of the night sky. States: Alaska (Juneau). Alaska and Hawaii weren't part of the United States yet in 1850; they're learned now to complete the fifty.
1838: Frederick Douglass escapes. 1849: Harriet Tubman escapes.
3–6 sentences in cursive: "Harriet Tubman." Literature's approved reading list this term includes The Drinking Gourd, which tells the same story for young readers.

Look back over the year: from a few settlements on the Atlantic coast in 1607 to a country stretching to the Pacific by 1850, with California just admitted as the 31st state. Narrate: "How did the country change between Jamestown and 1850?"
Color the 31 states of 1850 on a blank map of today's fifty. State: Hawaii (Honolulu), the last of the fifty.
1850: California becomes the 31st state. Read the whole year's timeline aloud from 1492 to 1850.

Looking ahead: tell the child that next year, the Modern year, begins with the Civil War, the inventions that changed the country, and the century after. Lincoln, whom they meet in Literature this term, will be at the center of it.
